notes: \cpara{The epigraph is the author's own, from the tenth virtue, precision, in ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006).}
\cpara{Gives three examples of people who draw fine distinctions in their own trades: the mechanic, the hunter-gatherer, the janitor.}

\cpara{States the fault the post opposes: outside their trades, people ``often'' stretch a word as wide as it will go. The reason is supplied by the post, in rhetorical questions: a general theory sounds loftier than an answer to a specific question.}

\cpara{The parable decides the question in advance. The pebbles the curious pick really are diamonds, so whoever wants to widen the name is wrong by construction. In a real dispute over a word, whether the other pebbles share the ``inner qualities'' is the open question, and the parable gives no way to settle it.}
\cpara{Extends the point to poets: even connotation needs precise tracking, as in choosing a flower with thorns to stand for jealous love.}
\cpara{Restates the parable as the thesis: attending to what a few special pebbles share ``is not a sin.''}

\cpara{The post names no one who reasons from the shared word to ``the same thing,'' and the shared word shows nothing by itself. ``Stellar evolution'' is astronomers' standard term for how a star changes over its life, and it implies no natural selection. The word's general sense, ``a process of change in a certain direction : unfolding'' (Merriam-Webster), is older than the biological one: the Online Etymology Dictionary dates the word in English to the 1620s and its use for the development of species to 1832.}
\cpara{Mocks ``Everything is connected to everything else'' as Deep Wisdom. The argument against it comes in the next paragraph.}

\cpara{The argument, and it is sound. A graph with every edge and a graph with no edges are complements of each other, and neither says which things are related to which. What informs is a pattern that joins some things and not others.}
\cpara{Says that endless verbal comparison connects everything, and that detailed study removes the false connections.}

\cpara{Carries the point from categories to hypotheses: a good one excludes some outcomes. This is Karl Popper's criterion, uncredited here as in ``Your Strength as a Rationalist'' (see the notes there).}

\cpara{Newton's gravity is the standard case of a theory that joined things thought separate: the fall of bodies on Earth, the orbits of the planets, the tides. It is a law about all the apples in the world. It excludes money and blood, as the post says, but its achievement was a new connection. Two paragraphs earlier the post said that detailed study leads to ``subtracting edges.'' The example shows that a category is judged by which things it joins as well as by which it leaves out; the post does not say how to judge either.}

\cpara{Socrates is answering Glaucon's praise of astronomy (529a--c). His complaint is against astronomy done by gazing at the sky instead of by mathematics; Paul Shorey's note on the passage calls it ``Plato's exasperation at the sentimentalists who prefer star-gazing to mathematical science.'' The passage says nothing of manual labor or slaves, the link the post draws. The translation is not named; it is neither Jowett's nor Shorey's, though the sense agrees with both.}
\cpara{A closing aside, in capitals, that declines to argue against three broad uses of terms from the author's own field: artificial intelligence, the Singularity, superintelligence.}
